name: Zinc oxide
lead: Zinc oxide (ZnO) is an inorganic white powder used as a mineral UV filter in sunscreens and as a skin protectant in diaper-rash creams, barrier ointments and calamine lotion [1][2]. For appearance, it is the ingredient behind broad-spectrum mineral sunscreens: it absorbs and scatters UVA and UVB, which is how it helps limit sunburn, uneven pigmentation and photoageing, and the same compound forms the base of creams that calm and protect irritated skin. Wikipedia calls it a broad-spectrum UVA and UVB absorber and states it is photostable [1].

Zinc compounds have been used in ointments for a very long time; an Indian medical text, the Charaka Samhita, mentions a zinc salve for eyes and wounds [1]. As of 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were recognised as generally recognised as safe and effective (GRASE) sunscreen filters by the US FDA; the EU approved zinc oxide as a UV filter in 2016 [3].

Larger particles produce a white cast, so many modern sunscreens use nanoparticle or tinted forms; the nanoparticles are a separate entry on this wiki [1][3][4]. Most of the world's zinc oxide goes to rubber manufacturing rather than skincare, and research on the material extends into electronics and dentistry [1].

paras: As a sunscreen filter it absorbs UVA (320 to 400 nm) and UVB (280 to 320 nm) [1]. Early-2000s research found it superior to titanium dioxide between 340 and 380 nm [3]. Non-nano mineral sunscreens may leave an opaque white cast that consumers often reject, and people tend to apply them more thinly than chemical sunscreens [3]. Environmental advocates often recommend mineral sunscreens for coral reef protection as a precaution [3].

SPF, introduced in 1974 by Franz Greiter, measures protection against UVB-driven sunburn, so UVA coverage is judged separately, for example by the PPD method used in the Japanese PA rating or the UK Boots star rating.[3] The FDA's rules effective in 2012 define broad spectrum as UVA protection proportional to UVB protection, and EU rules require a UVA protection factor of at least one-third of the SPF to carry the UVA seal.[3] Titanium dioxide is described as protecting well but not covering the full UVA range, which is why zinc oxide is often used for long-UVA cover.[3]

Cosmetic formulators address white cast with tinted bases and with smaller particle sizes; the nanoparticle forms are covered in a separate entry.[4] In the US, labels do not need to disclose mineral nanoparticles, while EU labels must.[3]

It is used in products for diaper rash, eczema itch, contact dermatitis and acne, in baby powder, barrier creams, calamine lotion (mixed with about 0.5% iron(III) oxide) and athletic tape [1]. Most industrial zinc oxide goes into rubber manufacturing [1]. Zinc oxide is also an ingredient in dental materials such as zinc oxide-eugenol cements [5].

Zinc oxide occurs naturally as the mineral zincite, but most is made synthetically. It usually forms the hexagonal wurtzite crystal structure, melts with decomposition near 1,974 degrees C and dissolves in most acids and strong alkalis, which makes it amphoteric. It is thermochromic, turning yellow when hot and white again on cooling, and it is piezoelectric [1].

Industrial output is on the order of 100,000 tons a year. The indirect (French) process, which vaporises zinc metal and oxidises it in air, supplies most of it; the direct (American) process starts from impure ores or smelter by-products and gives a lower-purity product, and a wet chemical route is a small share [1]. Rubber is the largest use, followed by ceramics, paints, plastics and cosmetics. Zinc white pigment is also a component of mineral makeup, and zinc oxide is used as a zinc source in fortified foods [1].

Its wide band gap of roughly 3.3 to 3.4 eV gives strong UV absorption [1]. Fine particles show antibacterial activity, and proposed mechanisms include reactive oxygen species generation, release of zinc ions and membrane disruption [1][6].

In sunscreens, mineral filters work mainly by absorbing UV light, with some reflection and scattering. The 2000s-era comparison of the two mineral filters found zinc oxide superior to titanium dioxide between about 340 and 380 nm, while titanium dioxide protects well but does not cover the whole UVA range [3].

Reapplication of sunscreen is typically recommended about every two hours, and a higher SPF does not extend how long a product lasts on skin. People tend to apply mineral sunscreens less thickly than chemical ones, which reduces the protection actually received [3]. Sunscreen use can help prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, with little evidence that it prevents basal cell carcinoma [3].

The FDA's 2019 proposed rule would require broad-spectrum protection for products above SPF 15 and would cap labels at SPF 60; the agency had proposed an SPF 50 cap earlier, in 2007 and 2011, without adopting it as of August 2019. EU sunscreen labels are capped at SPF 50+ [3]. Nanoparticle use must be disclosed on EU labels but not US ones [3].

Wikipedia traces zinc oxide ointments to antiquity: the Indian Charaka Samhita (around 500 BC or earlier) mentions a probable zinc oxide salve for eyes and wounds, and Dioscorides described a zinc oxide ointment in the first century AD, with Galen and Avicenna later recommending it for ulcerating conditions.[1] In Europe, a smelter opened in Bristol in 1743, Guyton de Morveau proposed zinc white as a replacement for lead white around 1782, and Edme-Jean Leclaire began large-scale pigment production in Paris in 1845, which made the material widely available.[1] Zinc oxide mixed with about 0.5 percent iron(III) oxide became the pink calamine used in lotions, and the compound is also used for athletic tape and baby barrier creams.[1]

Wikipedia states that zinc oxide paste has been used for skin protection for thousands of years, and that a zinc salve for eyes and wounds appears in the Indian Charaka Samhita.[1][3] In February 2019 the FDA proposed sorting UV filters into three categories: generally recognised as safe and effective (GRASE), not GRASE for safety reasons, and not GRASE pending more data. By 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were classed as GRASE, and PABA and trolamine salicylate were removed over safety concerns.[3] In the EU, sunscreens are regulated as cosmetics under Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, which sets minimum SPF and UVA requirements and requires disclosure of nanoparticles, and zinc oxide became an approved EU UV filter in 2016.[3]

Hawaii passed a law in 2018 banning sales of sunscreens containing oxybenzone and octinoxate, and Palau, Key West, the US Virgin Islands and Bonaire have restrictions on some chemical filters. Mineral sunscreens are often promoted as a precaution for reefs, while the labels 'reef-safe' and 'reef-friendly' are unregulated and the link between real-world concentrations and laboratory findings is debated.[3]

Wikipedia's account of the material notes that a smelter opened in Bristol in 1743 and that by about 1850 zinc white paint was made across Europe, valued because it resisted sunlight, was not blackened by sulfur-bearing air and was non-toxic [1].

Wikipedia describes zinc oxide as non-toxic, nonirritating, nonallergenic and non-comedogenic, and the FDA lists it as GRAS as a food additive [1]. Inhaling high concentrations of fumes, for example while welding galvanised steel, can cause metal fume fever [1]. Laboratory work shows that nano zinc oxide can be toxic to aquatic organisms, largely through dissolved zinc, and to cells in culture [7][8]. In some sunscreens combining zinc oxide with small-molecule absorbers, UV degraded those absorbers and produced toxicity in zebrafish embryos [1].

Zinc oxide mixed with eugenol is a long-standing dental material for cements, root canal sealers and children's pulpectomy, and trials and systematic reviews compare it with calcium silicate sealers and other agents [5]. Skin protectant products carry a US over-the-counter indication to help prevent and treat diaper rash and protect chafed skin, with labels advising stopping use if symptoms worsen or last more than seven days [13].

Registered trials include a phase 4 trial of zinc oxide ointment for recurrent aphthous stomatitis (NCT07565181, n=100, completed 2025), a study of zinc oxide versus MEBO for pressure injuries (NCT07193849, n=76, recruiting), a terminated diaper-dermatitis study (NCT04101890) and a study of singlet oxygen after UVA exposure of skin (NCT05865431, n=17) [9][10][11][12]. Studies of zinc oxide as an oral supplement concern zinc nutrition rather than skin appearance.

The registered studies concern medical rather than cosmetic outcomes. The phase 4 trial for recurrent aphthous stomatitis enrolled 100 people, the study of zinc oxide versus MEBO in pressure injuries enrolled 76, and the terminated Healthy Baby Bottoms diaper-dermatitis study enrolled 5.[9][10][11] The singlet oxygen study measured reactive oxygen in 17 volunteers' skin after UVA exposure.[12] In dentistry, zinc oxide-eugenol is a long-established sealer and pulpectomy material, and randomized trials and systematic reviews compare it with calcium silicate sealers and other materials in children's teeth.[5]

Zinc oxide sunscreens are discussed in skincare communities as a mineral option for sensitive or acne-prone skin and for tinted formulations, set against concerns about white cast and thick texture. These reflect general sunscreen discussion rather than claims specific to the compound.

Skincare enthusiasts discuss sunscreen as a core anti-aging step, and mineral formulas with zinc oxide are named for sensitive skin and for people who prefer to avoid chemical filters, while others prefer chemical filters for their lighter feel and absence of cast.[3]

Because mineral sunscreen is the product category rather than a compound-specific claim, discussion tends to centre on tint, texture and cast, with tinted mineral formulas and smaller particle sizes named as ways of reducing visible whitening [3][4].

card.summary: Mineral UV filter and skin protectant with broad UVA/UVB coverage; also the base of diaper-rash and barrier creams.
card.note: Non-nano forms leave a white cast; nano forms are covered separately.

quick.overview:
Zinc oxide is a mineral powder used as a sunscreen filter and as a skin protectant in diaper-rash and barrier creams. It covers both UVA and UVB and is described as photostable.
As of 2021 it and titanium dioxide were the only FDA-recognised GRASE sunscreen filters. Larger particles leave a white cast.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UV light because of its wide band gap and also scatters some. In skin products it acts as a physical barrier.
quick.risks: It is generally described as non-irritating and non-comedogenic. Inhaled fumes can cause metal fume fever, and nano forms are studied for effects on aquatic life.

chain: Absorbs and scatters UVA and UVB on the skin surface
Less sun damage reaches the skin
Less sunburn, pigmentation and photoaging over time
angle.text: Zinc oxide is the mineral sunscreen filter people use for broad UVA and UVB cover, which is how it supports even skin tone and fewer sun-related lines over the years. It is also the base of barrier creams that calm and protect irritated skin.
